transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-11-21
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Flores (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (CTO, LatticeWare), Anna Gomez (ML Eng), Samir Khan (Platform), Claire Liu (Procurement)

Summary: Quick Optimize console walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV caching recommendations for LatticeWare's customer-facing chat pipeline. Went through cost model scenarios (steady vs burst QPS), discussed sessionization vs lookahead prefetch, and agreed to run a 2-hour pilot benchmark.

Topics covered: console optimize -> cost model export, batching windows, prefix (kay vee) cache hit patterns, TTLs, concurrency tradeoffs, fallback routing, security/SSO notes.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're gonna start — appreciate you all squeezing this in. quick intros?
[00:07] Ravi: sure, Ravi Patel, CTO at LatticeWare. we run the customer chat and recommendation pipeline; Anna and Samir are on for infra and ml.
[00:13] Anna: hi, Anna — ML. thanks.
[00:15] Samir: Samir here. procurement is Claire, she may chime in on timeline.
[00:18] Claire: yes hi, thanks.
[00:20] Maya: cool. Ethan from Redwood will do most of the console deep-dive, i'll own the cost model and next steps.
[00:26] Ethan: hey all, yeah i'll share my screen, going to demo the Optimize console and the preftech.. prefetching recommendations, apologies for my pronunciation, i always call it prefetch and kay-vee cache, sometimes kay vee cash.
[00:37] [00:37] Ethan: (screen share) starting with the model profile we onboarded last week — note, this is a 16k context model variant, we have two quant profiles attached.
[00:46] Ravi: quick Q up front — our production 95th p90 latency SLO is 350ms, peak QPS ~1.8k but bursts to 6k for promos. we care more about tail latency than absolute token cost.
[00:56] Maya: good call, we should look at batching windows vs prefetch to hit that tail. ok Ethan, show them the steady-state cost scenario.
[01:03] Ethan: right. opening the cost-simulator tab — input is your QPS histogram and session length dist. i'll load the example you shared, and toggle batching from 5ms to 30ms.
[01:15] Ethan: so with 5ms batching (lower latency) and no prefix cache, cost per 1M tokens sits at roughly $X1 (demo numbers), latency median about 120, p95 320 on this HW profile. when we add a prefix cache with 15s TTL and 40% hit rate, cost drops to ~$X0.6 and p95 improves to ~260.
[01:39] Anna: 40% hit rate seems optimistic — our sessions are pretty diverse. how did you model the hit rate?
[01:45] Ethan: yeah, it's based on sessionization heuristics and overlap in user sequences — the console uses your provided session keys and common prefix length to estimate. i ran a quick sim with your sample traces and got 18% hit on longer session windows.
[01:57] Anna: ok 18% is closer. what about lookahead prefetch vs session caching?
[02:02] Ethan: good question — lookahead prefetch trades some extra tokens for higher hit rate; effectively you'll precompute likely next-token prefixes. in our sim, lookahead with 1-token prefetch moved hit to 28% and increased token volume by ~6%, but lowered p95 by ~40ms.
[02:22] Ravi: is that safe for privacy? prefetching sounds like storing more user context.
[02:27] Maya: we don't store raw user content in Redwood's managed prefix cache in hosted mode; for private deployments you can use customer-managed KV or onboard an encrypted KMS. also we have TTLs and scrub rules — Ethan, can you surface the security doc?
[02:39] Ethan: sure — i pasted the link in chat earlier, but short version: in Dedicated/Private, the KV lives in your VPC, encrypted with your KMS; we support SOC2 controls and audit logs per request.
[02:51] Samir: good. on sizing — if we enable lookahead, what's the expected memory and network delta for our GPU fleet?
[02:58] Ethan: memory overhead is small for prefix index references, but if you do aggressive prefetch and keep a warm KV for many sessions it increases RAM and cache hotspots. in the console i show a projected need: ~0.6GB per 10k active sessions. that was modeled on our test hardware; your infra may differ.
[03:17] Anna: can the optimizer suggest TTL per customer segment? we have guest vs logged-in users.
[03:22] Ethan: yes, you can create rules — longer TTLs for logged-in, shorter for guest. console has a rules engine that ties to session keys. we actually demoed a ruleset template in the Optimize repo.
[03:33] [03:33] Ethan: jumping to batching: the sim shows diminishing returns after ~25ms because of queueing and cold-starts. however, at your burst pattern, increasing batching during off-peak and sticky low-latency windows in peak helps economics.
[03:46] Ravi: so for our bursts, you'd recommend dynamic batching + prefetch?
[03:50] Ethan: exactly — dynamic policy: route to low-latency lane (5ms) until concurrency hits threshold, then open 20ms batching window and activate prefix prefetch for sessions above threshold. this keeps p95 bounded and reduces cost.
[04:05] Anna: about the cost model numbers — you referenced $X1 etc. can we get a CSV we can plug into our internal finance models?
[04:10] Maya: yes, i'll send the export. it's the same CSV that the console generated when we ran your histogram — includes token counts, estimated infra GPU-hrs, and KV costs.
[04:19] Claire: procurement question — if we start with hosted but later shift to Private, is there migration work for the cache layer?
[04:25] Ethan: migration is supported; the console can export and rehydrate cache keys. main lift is network rules and KMS integration for private. we have a migration runbook.
[04:35] Samir: are there any gotchas on consistency with session affinity? we do multi-region routing.
[04:40] Ethan: multi-region does complicate caching; you'll want either cross-region replication for the KV or bind sessions to a region. with our smart router you can pin sessions or fallback to a cold model with acceptable latency. we showed a fallback policy earlier.
[04:54] Ravi: surmising — we want low p95 for chat, and keep cost <= $Y/month. what would you propose as a pilot?
[05:01] Maya: 2-hour pilot during a weekday low-traffic window, mirror a small % of traffic, run batching policies and prefetch at varying TTLs; Ethan will instrument the console and we'll provide a cost delta report.
[05:12] Ethan: i'll create the pilot runbook; plan: 1) baseline run 2) dynamic batching run 3) prefetch run 4) combined. each for 20 minutes plus buffer.
[05:23] Anna: what telemetry do you need from our side?
[05:26] Ethan: sample traces with session IDs (hashed ok), QPS over 1-min buckets, token distributions, and the 95/99 latency samples. you can drop them in the secure file share link Maya will send.
[05:37] [05:37] (brief crosstalk)
[05:45] Samir: small nit, in the console sim the model label was mis-identified as 'redwood-m-16k-opt' — is that a real tag?
[05:52] Ethan: ha yeah our auto-tagging sometimes mangles names; that was an alias. the important bit is the perf profile underneath.
[05:59] Ravi: any competitor notes? we looked at vendor X and they suggested horizontal autoscaling but no prefix cache.
[06:05] Maya: right, many vendors rely solely on raw autoscale; Redwood's value is combined cache + batching + routing policy to control unit economics.
[06:14] Claire: timeline — procurement needs a ballpark and contract terms, are you suggesting monthly or committed for Dedicated?
[06:20] Maya: for pilot start hosted monthly, if the economics look good we can discuss a committed reserved capacity (dedicated pool) for predictable throughput and lower unit cost. we'll include both worksheets in the doc.
[06:32] [06:32] Ethan: quick demo of the optimize console export (click) — here's the CSV, you can toggle HW profile, batching window and prefetch TTL to see cost delta live.
[06:43] Anna: hmm the TTL slider — can we set TTL based on session length percentile?
[06:48] Ethan: not as discrete rule today but you can script via the API; it's on our roadmap to add percentile-based TTL suggestions.
[06:55] Ravi: Any known regression risks when enabling prefetch? we've seen hallucination rates spike when the model context is stale.
[07:01] Ethan: good point. prefetch is best for deterministic assistant replies or retrieval-augmented scaffolding. for generative open prompts, we recommend conservative prefetch and stronger evals. Redwood Optimize ties regressions to prompt eval sets and will alert if quality shifts.
[07:17] Anna: can we add a prompt set of 200 examples to the eval and gate prefetch rollouts?
[07:21] Maya: yes, we'll set up a canary with eval gating in the rollout policy.
[07:25] Claire: procurement: can you provide an SOC2 and DPA before pilot?
[07:29] Maya: yes, i'll share SOC2, DPA template, and network KMS integration docs in the follow-up.
[07:36] Ethan: last demo snippet — here's a run from another customer where prefetch + dynamic batching cut token cost by 34% in steady state while keeping p95 within SLO. figures vary.
[07:49] [07:49] Ravi: great. let's lock the pilot dates. Anna and Samir will sync with Ethan offline and we'll get Claire the procurement items.
[07:58] Maya: recap: i'll send cost CSV and paperwork; Ethan to create pilot runbook and propose 11/30 window; Ravi to share traffic histograms.
[08:09] Ethan: noted. any other questions?
[08:13] Anna: none from me.
[08:15] Claire: not right now.
[08:17] Maya: thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with attachments.
[08:21] End of call.

Notes on transcript quality: background noise minimal, occasional transcription mismatches (prefetch/kay-vee cache) and mis-tagged model aliases.
